title: Building on Soft Soil and Filled Ponds: Risks and Remedies
desc: Risks of building on filled ponds and paddy land, how to spot soft soil, common foundation solutions and what owners should do to prevent settlement and cracks.
summary: The risks of building on soft or filled ground, the foundation solutions engineers commonly consider, and points for protecting neighbouring houses.
body: p

Many new residential areas have been formed on filled ponds, lakes, rice fields and ditches. This ground is often weak, unconsolidated and settles unevenly. If a house is built as it would be on good soil, it may settle, tilt and crack within just a few years.
h2
1. Risks of building on soft soil
ul
Large, prolonged settlement: layers of mud and soft clay are gradually compressed over time.
Differential settlement: part of the house sits on fill and part on original ground, causing diagonal wall cracks and a tilting house.
Yard and floor slabs sink away from the wall bases, and pipes break.
Impact on neighbouring houses when deep foundations are excavated, groundwater is lowered or piles are driven.
h2
2. Signs that a plot may be weak
ul
Ask long-time residents whether it used to be a pond, field, ditch or dump.
The ground is soft and water stands for a long time after rain; the groundwater level is high.
Surrounding houses show cracks, tilting, or sunken yard slabs.
The fill is recent and has not had time to stabilise.
p

These signs are only warnings. To know for sure, a geological survey is needed – construction surveying includes engineering-geological and hydrogeological surveys under Article 21 of the Construction Law 2025.
h2
3. Solutions engineers commonly consider
ul
Use a pile foundation to transfer loads to the good soil layer below, rather than “placing” the house on the weak layer.
A raft or intersecting strip foundation to spread loads evenly and reduce differential settlement, where the weak layer is fairly uniform and the house is not too heavy.
Ground improvement (replacing soil, or reinforcing by suitable technical solutions) in some cases.
Reducing the building load: choosing lighter materials for walls, floors and roof where appropriate.
Settlement joints between building blocks with different loads or ground.
p

The choice of solution depends on the survey results, the building's loads, neighbouring houses and cost. This is a job for a structural engineer; owners should not decide on the basis of word-of-mouth experience.
h2
4. Protecting adjoining houses
p

The owner of a private house is responsible for the safety of adjacent works during construction; the supervision content includes safety measures for the house and adjoining works (Clauses 3 and 4, Article 10 of Decree 207/2026/ND-CP). It is advisable to photograph and record the condition of the neighbour's house before starting; when driving piles or excavating foundations, monitor cracks and settlement. See also Building causes a neighbour's house to settle or crack: liability and compensation.
h2
5. What owners should do
ol
Find out the history of the plot before buying or building.
Commission a geological survey and hire a design firm experienced with soft ground.
Budget for foundations that cost more than for a house on good soil; do not cut back on this part.
Record the condition of adjoining houses and monitor them throughout construction.
Monitor settlement after completion; if you see abnormal cracks or tilting, have an engineer check early.
p
Was your plot once a pond or a field? Contact Quan Construction for advice on a suitable foundation solution.
note

This article is for reference; every building needs to be surveyed and designed by qualified professionals. The principles above do not replace the drawings, technical instructions and calculations of the structural engineer for each specific house.
